title: Go to their house (Berakhot 28a)
hookLine: Gamliel visits Rabbi Joshua, sees his poverty, and asks forgiveness
tomorrow: a sick teacher is asked for the paths of life. what's his first?

cards: Sorry by text takes a few seconds. Type, send, phone face-down, and you never have to see their face. Rabban Gamliel, just removed from his seat, picks the slow way.
I'll go, he says, and make peace with Rabbi Joshua. No message through a student. He walks to the house.

teach.b: Today's question is old: when you've wronged someone, where does the apology happen? The Talmud answers with a scene. At the house, Gamliel sees the walls are black with soot.
From your walls, he says, it seems you make charcoal for a living.
Joshua answers sharply: woe to the generation whose leader you are, for you don't know the struggles of the scholars, how they earn a living and how they eat.
Gamliel says: I've humbled myself before you; forgive me. Joshua doesn't answer. Gamliel asks again, for the honor of his father's house, and Joshua forgives.
Notice what the visit did. From his seat, Gamliel never saw the soot.

teach.h: YOM KIPPUR WAITS FOR THE PERSON.
teach.b: The Mishnah puts the rule plainly: Yom Kippur atones for wrongs between a person and God, but wrongs between people wait until you make peace with the person. Here's something Jews share with a neighbor.
Christians read it in Matthew's Gospel, in the words of Jesus: "Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift."

In both, the person you hurt comes before the offering. One honest difference: for Christians it's Jesus teaching in the Sermon on the Mount; the Mishnah ties it to Yom Kippur, the day Jews fast and ask forgiveness.
And the line to tell a friend tonight: the apology wasn't only the words.
It was the walk to the house.

how: It is a Jewish custom, especially before Yom Kippur, to seek out people you've wronged and ask their forgiveness in person, following the Mishnah's teaching that wrongs between people need the person's pardon.

games.q: what does “go to their house” mean?
o: apologize face to face, where the other person lives
invite the person you wronged over to your place
visit a sick friend at home and bring them a meal

p: you don't know how scholars live
first be reconciled to thy brother

s: on Yom Kippur, wrongs against other people are forgiven automatically
the Mishnah says wrongs between people wait until you make peace with the person.
Rabbi Joshua forgave Gamliel the moment he asked
Joshua didn't answer at first; Gamliel asked again, for his father's honor.
Matthew's Gospel also puts making peace before the offering
leave there thy gift before the altar; first be reconciled to thy brother.

games.q: you're Jewish, your coworker is Christian, and you both owe the same teammate an apology after a rough meeting. which first step could you both stand behind?
o: go to the teammate, face to face, before anything else.
pray about it privately; the teammate doesn't need to hear it.
send one group message, so neither of you has to go alone.
games.why: the Mishnah: wrongs between people wait for the person. Matthew: leave thy gift, first be reconciled to thy brother. different books, a shared first step.

practice: On paper, write the name of one person you owe an apology, and the first sentence you'd say at their door. Under it, write where you could say it in person. The paper is only the map; the walk is the apology.

wordCard.voice: Go to their house. Gamliel walks to Rabbi Joshua's, sees how he lives, asks twice, and is forgiven.

orig.note: Hebrew, Mishnah Yoma: until he makes peace with his fellow. Yom Kippur waits for that.

carryVoice: Your line: go to their house. Words help, but the walk is the apology. Seventeen of fifty.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 28a (Rabban Gamliel goes to Rabbi Joshua's house, sees the blackened walls, asks forgiveness)
Mishnah Yoma 8:9 (Yom Kippur atones between a person and God; between people, only once the other is appeased)

sources.q: Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift.
